$about: Three L3 adoptions against trending Python repositories, 2026-08-07: simonw/llm, pydantic/pydantic-ai and Textualize/textual. Python has no registered stack, so all three also exercise the honest-miss path - the second, third and fourth times it has been walked against a real repository, and the first three times end to end rather than as a dry run. Every number below was produced by running the shipped scripts against the adopted working copy, or by running the target's own documentation build; none was read out of a method doc. All three adoptions live on local branches. Nothing was pushed to any of the three repositories and no issue or pull request was opened against them.

$elicitation.$why: This corpus measures whether the tooling conforms - gates, manifests, drift counts. No person was prompted in any of these runs and none was meant to be, so it evidences nothing about whether the standard asks anybody anything. It was never labelled that way, which is how 377 green observations came to read as validation of a product whose central promise is being guided.

observations.evidence: First run with only the copy-class guards and the manifest in place: 'self-verify: drift 15 - 63% adopted (26/41)' at the core profile. Final run after wave one: 'self-verify: OK - drift 0 - 100% adopted (43/43), 0 excepted'. The denominator moves 41 -> 43 because entries that cannot be checked until a prior artifact exists become checkable once it does. Every one of the 15 was closeable by authoring rather than by exception - no entry turned out to be inapplicable to a Python CLI, including the ones written for a Node-shaped tree. Worth stating plainly for a Python repo: the guards are dependency-free Node scripts, so alignment installed a Node runtime requirement into a project whose own toolchain is uv and pytest. The router says so at intake and it held.

2,324 tracked files, 2,653 commits, 551 contributors, first commit 2024-06-14. First run: 'self-verify: drift 16 - 68% adopted (34/50)' at the scale profile. Final: 'self-verify: OK - drift 0 - 100% adopted (53/53), 0 excepted'. Two of the sixteen were `requiredKeys` failures on a `.claude/settings.json` the repository already had - permissions.deny and hooks.PreToolUse - which is the merge class working as designed: the repository's own 21-entry allow list survived the merge untouched and the standard's deny list and hooks were added beside it. The `.claude/skills` copy-class directory entry also behaved: it reported '20 missing of 20 shipped files' and said nothing about the seven skills the repository already had, which is the difference between a copy entry and an overwrite.

2,120 tracked files, 13,103 commits, 202 contributors, first commit 2021-04-08. First run: 'self-verify: drift 15 - 66% adopted (29/44)' at the scale profile. Final: 'self-verify: OK - drift 0 - 100% adopted (47/47), 0 excepted'. This was the one repository of the three with no AGENTS.md at all, so the agent entry point was authored rather than merged. Its CHANGELOG.md is Keep a Changelog, which specifies an `## Unreleased` heading, so R18's section requirement fitted the repository's existing convention exactly - the only one of the three where the changelog entry cost nothing to reconcile.

The brownfield phase's own intermediate state does not survive the guard the same phase tells the adopter to wire up. onboard.md step 2 says map every capability, step 5 says a capability not specced this pass is a backlog item and explicitly forbids writing a placeholder spec to look done, and step 8 says wire the guards forward. Following all three literally: a ten-capability map (three published packages are a capability each; pydantic_ai_slim decomposes one level down), one capability specced, and 'spec-guard --audit: 9 problem(s)' - all nine of the form 'map entries naming a capability that has no spec'. The unclaimed check was fully on and green and every glob matched, so the audit's other three checks were satisfied; the only thing red was the designed state. The shipped .github/workflows/spec-guard.yml runs `--audit --block` on every pull request, deliberately at every profile, so this blocks from the moment the workflow lands until every capability is specced - which is precisely the big-bang the phase forbids. The escape was measured on the same tree at the same commit: a map naming only the one specced capability, with everything else declared under $unclaimed, reports 'spec-guard --audit: OK (1 capability specs, all mapped; 2 globs, all matching; 2324 files, each claimed by a capability or declared unclaimed)'. Green, and 2,287 of those 2,324 files - everything but the 37 the one remaining capability claims, including the entire 287-file agent framework - are green because they were declared to belong to no capability. So the audit is red on the honest map and green on the one that says nothing. Reproduced at two other scales: llm, 7 capabilities and 3 specced, 4 problems; textual, 8 capabilities and 1 specced, 7 problems. Not fixed - the resolution is a design decision, and the options are written out in the waiver below.
observations.waiver: Open by design, not a silent gap: measured this round, not built. Options, none taken this round. (a) Give the audit a third verdict for a mapped-but-unspecced capability - a note rather than a problem - and let R11's real invariant (no capability outside the map) stay blocking; the cost is that a genuinely forgotten spec stops being loud. (b) Let the map declare an intended spec explicitly, e.g. a `$pending` list or a per-entry flag, so 'not yet' is a recorded state rather than an absence; the cost is a new manifest-shaped concept. (c) Keep the audit as it is and change onboard.md to say the map grows with the specs, one capability at a time; the cost is that R11 stops holding during the whole wave programme, which is exactly when the map would be most useful. (d) Keep both and stop running --audit blocking in the shipped workflow at the core profile; the cost is that the check people most need on a brownfield repo is the one they no longer run.

observations.evidence: The manifest roots 16 entries at docs/, 12 of them core-profile. In this repository docs/ is the published Sphinx source: .readthedocs.yaml points at docs/conf.py, exclude_patterns is only ['_build', 'Thumbs.db', '.DS_Store'], and README.md itself is generated from docs/index.md. Measured with the repository's own docs/requirements.txt in a clean venv: the baseline build reports 'build succeeded, 14 warnings' (all 14 are autodoc import failures because llm is not installed in the docs venv - environmental, not repository defects). A single probe file at docs/PRINCIPLES.md takes it to 15, the new one being "docs/PRINCIPLES.md: WARNING: document isn't included in any toctree", and PRINCIPLES.html is written into the published output. After the full adoption the build reports 30 warnings. The 16 new ones break down exactly: 7 x 'document isn't included in any toctree' (one per governance page, each of which is also published to llm.datasette.io), 4 x "Unknown source document '../backlog'", 3 x "Unknown source document '../specs/<cap>/spec'", and 2 x "'myst' cross-reference target not found: '_template.md'". The last nine are cross-references between the taxonomy's own artifacts: a persona roster and a decision record naturally cite the backlog and the specs they relate to, and both of those live outside docs/ - so a docs engine reading docs/ as its source root cannot resolve any link that leaves it. The shipped templates carry no such link themselves; the links appear the moment the artifacts are authored, which is the point. The manifest offers no alternative root and altPaths exists on only four entries, none of them under docs/. The adopter's options are to publish their governance tree, to break their docs build, or to write a wall of exceptions - and an exception never raises the adoption percentage, so a repository that legitimately cannot use docs/ can never read as fully adopted.
observations.waiver: Open by design, not a silent gap: measured this round, not built. The resolution is a manifest-shape decision the owner has to make, and the options carry different costs. (a) Give the docs/-rooted entries declared altPaths under a non-published root, the way CHANGELOG.md and backlog.md already have two spellings each; cheapest, and it multiplies the number of places a reader has to look for a governance document. (b) Let the manifest copy declare one docs root the entries are relative to, so a repository sets it once; a new manifest concept, and every tool that hard-codes 'docs/' has to learn it. (c) Move the governance tree out of docs/ in the shipped tree entirely - say .standards/ or governance/ - which fixes every docs-engine repository at once and breaks the path every existing adopter already carries. (d) Do nothing and document the collision plus the per-engine exclusion recipe (Sphinx exclude_patterns, mkdocs exclude_docs); no code, and it leaves a repository that legitimately cannot use docs/ unable ever to read as fully adopted, because an exception never raises the percentage.

observations.evidence: Same collision, harder consequence. mkdocs.yml sets 'strict: true' and 'validation: omitted_files: warn', and the production docs build - the Makefile's cf-pages-build target - runs 'uv run mkdocs build' with no --no-strict (the local 'docs' and 'docs-serve' targets pass --no-strict and carry a comment saying why). Under those settings a docs page that is not in nav is a warning, and strict mode turns a warning into a failure. Demonstrated on a minimal fixture with the same two settings: 'WARNING - The following pages exist in the docs directory, but are not included in the "nav" configuration: - personas.md' followed by 'Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!', exit 1. So for this repository landing the manifest's docs/ entries does not add warnings, it breaks the documentation deployment until every governance page is added to nav, added to exclude_docs, or moved out of docs/ entirely. Recorded in the adopted repository's own backlog as DOCS-1 rather than worked around.
observations.waiver: Same waiver as the llm observation - one decision covers all three targets. Recorded separately because the consequence differs in kind: warnings on a Sphinx build, a failed deployment on a strict mkdocs build.

observations.evidence: Third repository, third mkdocs/Sphinx docs root - this one with four config files (mkdocs-common.yml, mkdocs-nav.yml, mkdocs-online.yml, mkdocs-offline.yml) and the nav held in its own file. Three for three: every Python repository in this round keeps its published documentation source at docs/, which is the ordinary convention for the ecosystem, and the manifest's 16 docs/-rooted entries collide with it every time. This is not a property of one repository's taste.
observations.waiver: Same waiver as the llm observation. Recorded as the third independent confirmation that this is an ecosystem convention rather than one repository's taste.

observations.evidence: Re-confirmed at L3, having previously only been checked by reading the tree. Executing the honest-miss path end to end: 'stack-decisions' appears in backlog.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, ADR-021, the stack-request issue template, greenfield.md, SKILL.md and the validation data - and in none of standard.manifest.json, standard/SPEC.md or docs/method/taxonomy.md. Consequences that only surface when the document is actually produced: (1) there is no template, and the router's instruction is to shape it 'like the node stack's DECISIONS', a file in a repository a core-only adopter was never told to clone - so the shape had to be reconstructed from a checkout that happened to be on this machine; (2) the finished document does not move the drift number in either direction. All three repositories reached 'drift 0 - 100% adopted' with docs/stack-decisions.md present, and would have reported the identical number with it deleted. The one deliverable the entire Layer 2 path produces for an unregistered technology is invisible to the only mechanism that says whether adoption happened.
observations.waiver: Open since 2026-08-04 and still open; this round moves it from a dry-run finding to an executed one and adds a consequence the earlier rounds could not see - the document is produced, is useful, and does not move the drift number in either direction. The fix is the one ADOPT-07 has always named (a manifest entry, a SPEC rule or a taxonomy row, plus a template so the shape does not have to be reconstructed from another repository's file), and it is a deliberate owner decision about whether an unregistered-technology record is a required deliverable or an optional one. Making it required would mean every adopter on a registered stack carries an entry that does not apply to them, which is why it is not a one-line change.

observations.evidence: The document itself is usable, which is the half worth recording as working. Written against measured evidence rather than blog consensus, it found that this repository already satisfies most of what a Python stack would prescribe - uv with a committed lock and --frozen installs, ruff, pyright, 715 of 727 workflow `uses:` references pinned to full commit SHAs, Trusted Publishing with the publish action itself SHA-pinned, and '[tool.uv] exclude-newer = "7 days"', a dependency cooldown most Python projects do not have. Recording agreements is as much of the deliverable as recording gaps: those rows exist so the next reviewer does not re-argue them. The contrast across the three targets is the evidence that the fallback produces something real rather than a template: llm's row set came out with four open items (unpinned actions, no cooldown, two formatters, a default-only ruff rule set), pydantic-ai's with one, textual's with a two-lockfile problem neither of the others had. Still `partial` rather than `pass` because the mechanical half of ADOPT-07 is unchanged - no manifest entry, no SPEC rule, no taxonomy row, no template.

The consent gate held, and it is worth being precise about what held it. The router's step 5 says to offer to file a stack request upstream, 'consent-gated, never automatic'. No issue was filed. But nothing in the tree would have stopped one: the gate is a sentence in a skill file plus the operator's discipline, and .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/stack-request.yml is a template an agent with a gh token can fill in without asking anyone. Compare the mechanically-held gates in the same tree - the clarify gate is a script that exits non-zero, the coupling guard reads a diff - and this one is prose. The draft it would have filed is real and ready (technology: python; evidence: pyproject.toml in all three repositories, no stacks.json entry, three independently produced docs/stack-decisions.md files as seed material), and it stays undelivered because consent was never given. Also worth recording: stacks.json's own $about names 'repository-standards/python' as an example of the naming policy, so a router that greps the file for the technology rather than reading its stacks array finds a false hit for exactly this case.

onboard.md offers two shortcuts for deriving a capability map - 'an existing package/crate boundary is often already the capability map' for a workspace, and 'a single-package micro-library has no package boundary to inherit from - look one level down'. This repository is both at once and neither shortcut says so: a uv workspace of five members where three (pydantic_graph, pydantic_evals, clai) genuinely are one capability each, and the fourth, pydantic_ai_slim, is 287 tracked files and the whole framework. Taking the workspace shortcut literally produces a four-entry map whose largest entry covers the product. The repository had, however, already written its own internal boundaries down: eight directory-scoped AGENTS.md files under pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/ - capabilities/, durable_exec/, models/, native_tools/, profiles/, providers/, toolsets/, ui/ - each stating that directory's behavioural rules (13 AGENTS.md files across the whole repository). Those are the capability boundaries, authored by the maintainers, in a form onboard.md does not look for: it looks at package manifests, not at where a repository chose to put its own agent instructions. The final map has ten entries and the audit reports every glob matching and every one of 2,324 files claimed or declared.

The opposite shape and a harder limit: a single package where one file, llm/cli.py, is 4,306 lines and implements every command group in the tool - prompt, chat, keys, logs, models, templates, schemas, tools, aliases, fragments, plugins, embed, collections. Seven capabilities were derived from behaviour, and llm/cli.py belongs to all of them. The coupling map's unit is a file glob, so a glob cannot address part of a file: the honest map claims llm/cli.py under all seven, which means any edit to it demands seven spec updates before spec-guard passes. The alternatives are worse - declaring the largest behaviour file in the repository under $unclaimed, or minting a 'command-line-interface' capability, which is the layering artifact ADR-002 and onboard.md step 2 both forbid. Recorded in the adopted repository's backlog as GUARD-2. This is not a defect in the map's design so much as an unstated precondition of it: the coupling guard's usefulness is bounded by the repository's file granularity, and nothing in onboard.md warns that a monolithic entry-point module will make the guard either coarse or noisy.

Second confirmation on a much bigger tree, and the caveat from the first one holds. Declaring $unclaimed turned the check on and it did the work: it named .agents/skills/ (a second skills tree the repository keeps beside .claude/skills/), .gemini/config.yaml, .macroscope/ignore.md, tests/assets/, tests/example_modules/ and tests/profiles/ - the last of which was a genuine mapping error on my part, not an exemption, and claiming it under model-providers was the right fix. It also caught four globs matching nothing (tests/capabilities/**, tests/durable_exec/**, tests/ui/**, tests/embeddings/**) because I had assumed a per-capability test directory layout the repository does not use. The final line reads '2324 files, each claimed by a capability or declared unclaimed'. The caveat: as on the first run, none of this is discoverable without adding the key - the audit's own output is the only place the feature is mentioned.

onboard.md step 5 requires that an unclear branch or a spec-code discrepancy be recorded in the spec's Open questions rather than guessed. The structure guard re-runs the clarify gate on any spec claiming ready-to-develop or live, and the clarify gate fails closed on a single open [NEEDS ...] marker. Both are right on their own terms and together they have one consequence: a spec honestly reconstructed from three years of shipped code must be labelled in-refinement. Measured - setting Status: live on specs/prompt-execution/spec.md, which carries two open markers, produces 'spec-structure: specs claiming a status the clarify gate does not grant: - specs/prompt-execution/spec.md says `live`'. So specs/ cannot distinguish a spec of code running in production with two questions open from a draft of something nobody has built; both read in-refinement. All three adoptions in this round shipped every spec as in-refinement for exactly this reason, describing code with 13,103, 2,653 and 1,245 commits behind it. Not fixed - the fix is a vocabulary decision. Options: add a status meaning 'live, spec incomplete'; or let a live spec carry open markers when a separate field records that the code ships regardless; or state in onboard.md that in-refinement is the correct and permanent brownfield value and say what a reader should infer from it, which is the cheapest and the least satisfying.
observations.waiver: Open by design, not a silent gap: measured this round, not built. The fix is a vocabulary decision. (a) Add a status meaning 'live, spec incomplete', which makes specs/ readable at a glance and adds a value every downstream reader has to learn. (b) Let a live spec carry open markers when a separate field records that the code ships regardless, which keeps the enum small and splits the meaning across two fields. (c) State in onboard.md that in-refinement is the correct and permanent value for a reconstructed brownfield spec and say what a reader should infer, which costs nothing and fixes nothing. Left to the owner because the status enum is read by the structure guard, the spec template and three skills.

observations.evidence: The repository ships AI_POLICY.md, the file the intake's red-flag-stop branch was written against (it names BurntSushi/ripgrep's). This one is not a ban. Quoted in full, it accepts AI-generated pull requests provided the PR fills in the template, 'must identify itself as AI generated, including the name of the agent used', and 'must link to a issue or discussion where a solution has been approved by a maintainer (@willmcgugan)' - with the maintainer reserving the right to close PRs without comment otherwise. SKILL.md step 0 has exactly two branches: a stop for a ban, and a conditional allow for a policy demanding human authorship, disclosure, or no verbatim pasted output. This is a third kind: not a condition on who writes the contribution but on what must already have happened before it exists. The conditional-allow remedy - hand every artifact to the human to review and rewrite before submitting - does not satisfy it, because a human rewriting the branch still has no approved issue behind it. And the router's step 7 ('Open one focused PR') has no branch for a repository where the first deliverable is a discussion rather than a change. An adoption pull request is by definition large and unsolicited, so under this policy the correct first artifact is a proposal. The intake read the file and stopped; the branch it needed was not there, so the judgement was the operator's rather than the procedure's - which is the finding.
observations.waiver: Open by design, not a silent gap: measured this round, not built. The fix is a third branch in SKILL.md step 0 plus a matching branch at step 7, and it is a wording addition rather than a mechanism - but it needs the owner to decide what the router should produce when a repository's policy makes a discussion the first deliverable rather than a pull request. The candidate answer is that align produces the proposal (the assessment's health report and counted plan are already exactly that material) and stops there, which is close to the assessment-only outcome the intake already has a name for - so the cheap version may be to route this case to assessment-only and say why.

observations.evidence: Found during the adoption and fixed in the same change. The repository keeps a 1,137-line hand-written changelog at docs/changelog.md, published at llm.datasette.io, and the CHANGELOG.md manifest entry declares altPaths ['docs/CHANGELOG.md'] for exactly this situation. Isolated in a three-entry fixture: with the file at the declared alternate, self-verify printed 'PASS file CHANGELOG.md' and immediately 'FAIL section CHANGELOG.md missing, so "Unreleased" cannot be checked' - drift 1 on a file that was not missing, with no way to close it except moving the file to the path the altPath exists to avoid. The file check resolved altPaths; the section check read only the primary name. Fixed by resolving a section through its file entry's altPaths, keeping the exception key on the canonical name so a recorded deviation still matches; the fixture now reports 'PASS section docs/CHANGELOG.md > "Unreleased"', drift 0. Three cases in tools/self-verify-drift-test.mjs cover it both ways - the altPath resolves, a heading genuinely absent from the altPath copy still fails naming that file, and a changelog absent from every declared path still reports its section as uncheckable. The first two fail against the pre-fix script; the third passes both, which is what makes it the regression guard. Landed in: standard/scripts/self-verify.mjs - a section resolves through its file entry's declared altPaths; three cases in tools/self-verify-drift-test.mjs. The fix ships in the same change as this record; its pull request is not merged yet, which is why no `fix` field is set here - that field is a merged-PR URL and the page counts distinct values of it as merged pull requests.

Found by walking into it. Three ADRs were authored, decision-records-check named all three as unindexed, index rows were added as '| [ADR-001](ADR-001-plugins-are-the-extension-mechanism.md) | ... |' - the record's own id as the link label - and the guard reported the same three failures again, unchanged, with the rows sitting in the table two lines above. The cause: the first cell was matched against /^\[(\d+)\]\(([^)]+)\)$/, so a prefixed label matched neither the linked nor the bare form and the row was skipped entirely before any comparison happened. The shipped adr/README.md carries only a placeholder row '| - | (none yet) | - |', so the accepted syntax is documented nowhere an adopter reads, and the failure message pointed at the file rather than at the row. Fixed by making the ADR-/BDR- prefix optional in both cell forms, resolving a prefixed bare cell to the stream it names rather than guessing, and naming the four accepted forms in the failure message. Against the real adoption the guard then reported 'decision-records-check: OK (3 record(s), index and directory agree)'. Three cases in tools/decision-records-check-test.mjs, all three failing against the pre-fix guard. Landed in: standard/scripts/decision-records-check.mjs - the ADR-/BDR- prefix is accepted in both cell forms and the failure names them; three cases in tools/decision-records-check-test.mjs. The fix ships in the same change as this record; its pull request is not merged yet, which is why no `fix` field is set here - that field is a merged-PR URL and the page counts distinct values of it as merged pull requests.

The original case still fires on a third repository: two ADRs written into docs/decision-records/adr/ with the shipped placeholder index untouched, and decision-records-check --block named both and exited non-zero. After the rows were added: 'decision-records-check: OK (2 record(s), index and directory agree)'. Recorded separately from DOC-19 because they are different failures with the same symptom - one is a row that was never written, the other a row that was written in a shape the guard could not see.
